It is the case of the complainant that, accused No.1 duly represented by accused No.2 as a Managing Director and accused No.3 and 4 being the directors of the accused No.1 company.
Accused 2 to 4 persuaded the complainant to invest in the accused No.1 company and accordingly,
accused no.1 had received in a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- and issued the acknowledgment on 13.04.2018 to the complainant, further accused No.1 had received in a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- and issued the acknowledgment on 10.07.2019 to the complainant, while assuring in getting handsome periodical return and towards the repayment of the same, accused No.2 had issued a post dated cheque bearing No.254749, dated 08.10.2020, drawn on IDBI Bank, Basavanagudi, Bengalur- 560 004 for Rs.5,00,000/-, with a undertaking to honor both cheques without fail on its presentation.
3.

As per the instructions of accused No.2 to 4, the complainant did presented the aforesaid cheques for encashment on 08.10.2020, however, to her shock and dismay, the said cheques came to be returned for the reason "Funds Insufficient" from her banker i.e., Karur Vysya Bank Ltd.,
Rajajinagar Branch, Bengaluru.

Thereafter, she could able to get in touch with the accused No.2, but for avoidance in the matter, the complainant forced to cause Legal notice dated 15.10.2020 calling upon the accused to pay a sum of Rs.10,00,000/- along with interest @ 18% p.a. within 15 days from the receipt of the said notice.

The said notice has been sent to the accused No.1 to 3 were served on 16.10.2020 and on 17.10.2020, notice sent to accused no.4 were served on 21.10.2020 and for accused No.4 sent to another address return with shara "Addressee Left" on 19.10.2020.
The accused persons have not paid the cheques amount and have committed an offence punishable u/s 138 of NI Act.
Hence, this complaint.

4. After recording the sworn statement of the complainant by way of affidavit and also verifying the documents, cognizance was taken against the accused persons for the offence punishable under Sec.138 of N.I. Act.
The accused persons appeared before this Court through their respective counsels and enlarged on bail and their plea was recorded.
The accused persons pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.
Hence, the case was posted for evidence of the complainant.
5. The complainant got examined herself as PW.1 and got marked 19 documents as Exs.P.1 to Ex.P.19 and Ex.P19(a).
Thereafter, the case was posted for recording the statement of accused under Sec.313 of Cr.P.C.
In the statement U/s. 313 Cr.P.C., the accused persons have denied all the incriminating evidence appearing against them.
On the other hand, accused No.2 has examined himself as DW.1 and got marked documents as Ex.D1 to Ex.D14.
The accused No.2 also has examined as DW.2 and got marked documents as Ex.D15 to Ex.D23.

6. The learned counsel for accused No.1 to 3 has relied on the following Judgment:
1. Crl. Rev. Pet. No.408/2024 between P.C. Hari Vs. Shine Verghese dated 25.07.2025 passed by the Hon'ble High Court of Kerala.

Heard the arguments of both side and Perused the records.

Whether the complainant proves that the cheques bearing No.254749 and 230085 dated 08.10.2020 for Rs.5,00,000/- each drawn on IDBI Bank, Basavanagudi Branch, Bengaluru issued by the accused persons have been dishonored on the grounds of 'Funds Insufficient' and even after receiving the intimation regarding the dishonor of cheques failed to pay the cheques amount within the stipulated period and thereby the accused persons have committed an offence punishable under Sec.138 of N.I. Act?
2. What order?
9. My findings on the above points are as under:-
Point No.1: In the Affirmative Point No.2: As per final order for the following :: R E A S O N S ::
10. POINT No.1:- In view of the present legal position as held by our Hon'ble High Court as well as Apex Court of India in a catena of decisions as well as relevant provisions of the Act, this court has to see whether the complainant has complied all the requirements as contained in Sec.138 of NI Act so as to bring home the guilt of the accused for the alleged offence.
If so, whether the accused is able to rebut the legal presumption available to the complainant under Sec.139 of the Act by adducing probable defense or not.

However, it is held by the full bench of our Apex Court in the case of Rangappa Vs. Mohan reported in 2010 (1) DCR 706 that;
"The Statutory presumption man- dated by sec.139 of the Act, does in- deed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability.

entities.text: Rangappa Vs. Mohan reported in 2010 (1) DCR 706

sentences.text:
However, the presumption U/S 139 of the Act is in the nature of a rebuttable pre- sumption and it is open for the ac- cused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested".
11.

Therefore, in view of the above decision, once the cheque is admitted, the statutory presumption would automatically fall in favour of the complainant that, the alleged cheque was issued for discharge of an existing legally enforceable debt or liability against the accused and the burden will shift on to the accused to rebut the same.

INGREDIENTS OF OFFENCE AND DISCUSSION:-
12. Before dwelling into the facts of the present case, it would be apposite to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both sides.
In order to establish the offence under Section 138 of NI Act, the prosecution must fulfill all the essential ingredients of the offence.
Perusal of the bare provision reveals the following necessary ingredients of the offence:-

sentences.text: Second Ingredient:
The cheques were drawn by the drawer for discharge of any legally enforceable debt or other liability;
The accused can only be held guilty of the offence under Section 138 NI Act if the above-mentioned ingredients are proved by the complainant co-extensively.
Additionally, the conditions stipulated under Section 142 NI Act have to be fulfilled.
Notably, there is no dispute at bar about the proof of only first, third, and fifth ingredient.
The complainant had proved the original cheques vide Ex.P.1 and 2 which the accused persons had not disputed as being drawn on the account of the accused.
It was not disputed that the cheques in question was presented within its validity period.
The cheques in question were returned unpaid vide return memo vide Ex.P.3 and 4 due to the reason, "Funds Insufficient".

The complainant had proved the service of legal demand notice dated 15.10.2020 vide Ex.P.5 by bringing on record the postal receipts vide Ex.P.6 to 11,
Postal acknowledgments vide Ex.P12 to 16, RPAD cover vide Ex.P17, Acknowledgment dated 13.04.2018 vide Ex.P18, Acknowledgment dated 10.07.2019 vide Ex.P19 and Signature vide Ex.P19(a).
Thus, there is a dispute only with regard to the second ingredient to the offence.

As such,
the 1st,3rd,4th& 5th ingredient of the offence under section 138 of the NI Act stands proved.
14. As far as the proof of second ingredient is concerned, the complainant has to prove that the cheque in question was drawn by the drawer for discharging a legally enforceable debtor any liability.
In the present case, the issuance of the cheque in question is not denied.
As per the scheme of the NI Act, once the accused admits signature on the cheque in question, certain presumption are drawn, which result in shifting of onus.
Section 118(a) of the NI Act lays down the presumption that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration.
Another presumption is enumerated in Section 139 of NI Act.
The provision lays down the presumption that the holder of the cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or part, of any debt or other liability.
15. The combined effect of these two provisions is a presumption that the cheque is drawn for consideration and given by the accused for the discharge of debt or other liability.
Both the sections use the expression "shall", which makes it imperative for the court to raise the presumptions once the foundational facts required for the same are proved.
Reliance is placed upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, Hiten P. Dalal vs. Bratindranath Banerjee (2001) 6 SCC 16.

sentences.text: Further, it has been held by a three-judge bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Rangappa vs. Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441 that the presumption contemplated under Section 139 of NI Act includes the presumption of existence of a legally enforceable debt.
Once the presumption is raised, it is for the accused to rebut the same by establishing a probable defence.
17. The presumptions raised under Section 118(b) and Section 139 NI Act are rebuttable presumptions.

A reverse onus is cast on the accused, who has to establish a probable defence on the standard of preponderance of probabilities to prove that either there was no legally enforceable debt or other liability.

24. On perusal of the Ex.D6 to D.12 though it is clear that there were many cheque bounce cases pending between accused No.1 to 3 and accused No.4 and also between accused No.4 and wife of the accused No.2, even Civil case is also pending between accused No.2 and 3 and accused No.4.

But,
neither accused No.1 to 3 nor accused No.4 cannot absolve themselves from the liability to pay the cheques amount only on this ground as already the complainant has clearly established the investment of Rs.10,00,000/- in the 1 st accused company and also the issuance of the cheques for the repayment of the said amount.
Even accused No.1 to 3 have not disputing the issuance of the cheques and due of amount towards company.

Though there may be the several disputes between 4 among the directors of the company i.e., accused No.1 to 3 and accused No.4, but merely on that ground accused No.1 to 4 cannot be devoid of liability to pay the cheques amount.

Any amount of disputes between the directors of the company is a interse dispute and accused No.1 to 4 cannot absolve themselves from the liability to pay the cheques amount to the independent investors of their company on that ground only.
25. The director is liable only if their incharge and responsible for the companies business at the time the offence was committed.
Internal interest disputes between the directors don't automatically absolve them from liability under 138 of NI Act.
Liability is based on directors active role and responsibility for the company business at the time of the offence, not just their position or disagreements with other directors.
Codes require specific evidence to prove a directors active involvement in the commission of the offence to establish vicarious liability.
Directors are held liable vicariously, but this is contingent on the proof of their active role and not on internal company dispute.

26. Coming to the factual matrics of the present case, accused No.4 himself has clearly admitted about the fact that he was an Additional Director of the company and on his instigation complainant has invested Rs.5 lakhs in the company and he has issued the acknowledgment as per Ex.P16 for the receipt of the Rs.5,00,000/- amount towards share capital.

32. Merely because the petitioner is the accountant of the Company, it is not right to say that he cannot be held liable for the offence under S.138 of the Act.

Under S.138 read with S.141 of the Act,
every person incharge of and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company shall also be liable fore the punishment under S.138 of the Act.

In the case of a company, a person, who is incharge of and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, need not be a Director, Manager, Secretary or other officer of the company for committing an offence under S.138: Dev v. State of A.P.2002 Cr.L.J.4770 (Andh.Pra.).

Act?

9. My findings on the above points are as under:-
Point No.1: In the Affirmative Point No.2: As per final order for the following :: R E A S O N S ::
10. POINT No.1:- In view of the present legal position as held by our Hon'ble High Court as well as Apex Court of India in a catena of decisions as well as relevant provisions of the Act, this court has to see whether the complainant has complied all the requirements as contained in Sec.138 of NI Act so as to bring home the guilt of the accused for the alleged offence.
If so, whether the accused is able to rebut the legal presumption available to the complainant under Sec.139 of the Act by adducing probable defense or not.
INGREDIENTS OF OFFENCE AND DISCUSSION:-
12. Before dwelling into the facts of the present case, it would be apposite to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both sides.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The accused can only be held guilty of the offence under Section 138 NI Act if the above-mentioned ingredients are proved by the complainant co-extensively.
14. As far as the proof of second ingredient is concerned, the complainant has to prove that the cheque in question was drawn by the drawer for discharging a legally enforceable debtor any liability.
As per the scheme of the NI Act, once the accused admits signature on the cheque in question, certain presumption are drawn, which result in shifting of onus.
The provision lays down the presumption that the holder of the cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or part, of any debt or other liability.
15. The combined effect of these two provisions is a presumption that the cheque is drawn for consideration and given by the accused for the discharge of debt or other liability.
Both the sections use the expression "shall", which makes it imperative for the court to raise the presumptions once the foundational facts required for the same are proved.
Reliance is placed upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, Hiten P. Dalal vs. Bratindranath Banerjee (2001) 6 SCC 16.
Nagarathna N R vs Bhoosiri Chits Pvt Ltd on 8 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/15475685/
5 16.
Further, it has been held by a three-judge bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Rangappa vs. Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441 that the presumption contemplated under Section 139 of NI Act includes the presumption of existence of a legally enforceable debt.
Once the presumption is raised, it is for the accused to rebut the same by establishing a probable defence.
A reverse onus is cast on the accused, who has to establish a probable defence on the standard of preponderance of probabilities to prove that either there was no legally enforceable debt or other liability.
Any amount of disputes between the directors of the company is a interse dispute and accused No.1 to 4 cannot absolve themselves from the liability to pay the cheques amount to the independent investors of their company on that ground only.
25. The director is liable only if their incharge and responsible for the companies business at the time the offence was committed.
Internal interest disputes between the directors don't automatically absolve them from liability under 138 of NI Act.
Liability is based on directors active role and responsibility for the company business at the time of the offence, not just their position or disagreements with other directors.
Codes require specific evidence to prove a directors active involvement in the commission of the offence to establish vicarious liability.
Directors are held liable vicariously, but this is contingent on the proof of their active role and not on internal company dispute.
The present complaint being the complaint filed under Sec.
138 of the NI Act being summary in procedure this court cannot go into enquring about the internal disputes between the accused No.1 to 3 and accused No.4.
Moreover, as on date of transaction and issuance of cheques, accused No.4 was also one of director and signatory to the cheques.
32. Merely because the petitioner is the accountant of the Company, it is not right to say that he cannot be held liable for the offence under S.138 of the Act.
In the case of a company, a person, who is incharge of and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, need not be a Director, Manager, Secretary or other officer of the company for committing an offence under S.138: Dev v. State of A.P.2002 Cr.L.J.4770 (Andh.Pra.).
33.
In view of all the above discussions, it can be concluded that the complainant has established through cogent and convincing evidence the fact of issuance of the cheques for discharge of legality enforceable debt, which is dishonored for want of sufficient funds, issuance of legal notice within stipulated time, failure on the part of accused to repay the amount within stipulated period.
On the other hand, the accused has failed to rebut the presumption available to the complainant through probable evidences that would preponderate upon the evidence lead by the complainant.
Therefore,
the accused persons are held to have committed an offence punishable under Sec. 138 of N.I. Act.
